pgp_table_rederivation.method: verify_all_signatures.py re-run from scratch in a fresh isolated GNUPGHOME over the whole repository, then diffed file-by-file against round18's stored table. The stored JSON was not read as evidence.
pgp_table_rederivation.disclosed_change: round18's own control artifacts (work/control_C2_tampered.asc, work/control_C3_foreign.asc) are excluded from the enumerator so a deliberately tampered file and a foreign-key file cannot enter the corpus counts.

C3_foreign_key.measured: NO_PUBKEY for the foreign keyid, no GOODSIG

controls.why_C2_C3_matter: Without them a table of 192 PASSes says only that gpg ran. They are what make a FAIL in this table a fact.
controls.keyring_isolation: enforced in code: throwaway GNUPGHOME per run, importing only key blocks whose PRIMARY fingerprint is canonical; the script aborts if any other primary key is present, so a PASS cannot be manufactured from ambient GnuPG state

the_three_fails.cause: the mirror dropped the blank line separating the `Hash: SHA1` armor header from the body, so the message's first line is parsed as a header and excluded from the hashed data
the_three_fails.repaired_copy_in_tree: corpus/A-primary-artifacts/pgp/repaired/ky_2013-01-opening-book-code.repaired.asc (1538 bytes) PASSes with the identical signature packet
the_three_fails.verdict_under_prereg_rule: transport defect, not a canon failure
the_three_fails.operational_warning: A TWO-BYTE whitespace defect turns an authentic Cicada message into a BADSIG. Anyone running this repository's own declared authenticity test (KNOWLEDGE.json: authenticity_test) against a casually mirrored copy gets a FALSE NEGATIVE and may conclude a genuine message is a forgery. Three such files are in this tree right now.

no_sig_hazard.hazard: named like communications (e.g. 2012-01-book-code-poem.asc); any tool that globs **/*.asc picks them up as Cicada messages. In the tree since Round 10.

L1_crosscheck.target: round18/L1-toolchain/RESULTS.md finding F6: '46/46 curated 3301 PGP messages, 2012->2014, are GnuPG v1.4.11 (GNU/Linux)', supporting 'one environment, three years, no drift'
consequences: F6's denominator (46) and window (2012->2014) are both wrong; the window truncates the span at exactly the point where the version string changes, so the claim is true INSIDE its window while the headline drawn from it - 'one environment, three years, no drift' - is contradicted by the same directory's own later files

The signing toolchain changed TWICE, not once. Round 18's L8 recorded one change from the digest algorithm (SHA-1 x53 -> SHA-512 x1 at 2017-04-04). The armor Version header shows an EARLIER, independent change between 2014-04-02 and 2015-07-28. Two dated transitions from two independent fields; the later one is corroborated by both.
'CicadaPG v.3301' is hand-set - no GnuPG build emits it. It is a deliberately customised armor version on the final 2017-04-04 message, which is also the only SHA-512 one.

L1's CONCLUSION SURVIVES and the correction sharpens it: the 1.4.11 environment is now attested over 2012-01-05 to 2014-04-02, 818 days, covering the entire Liber Primus release window. Round 19's Phase-1 generator ranking is NOT weakened; the era attribution is tighter than L1 stated because its end is now bounded.

independent_convergence.what_R1_found: a non-ImageMagick chain (Ghostscript -> PIL with quality='keep') reproduces all four of LP2's discriminating JPEG fields, and GnuPG 1.4.11 shipped in at least 6 OS generations including Ubuntu 12.10, outside L1's stated 11.04-12.04 bracket
independent_convergence.significance: two lanes reached the same defect in L1's prior from different directions - R1 from the render/packaging side, C3 from the signed-corpus side. Convergent, independent evidence is much stronger than either alone, and it matters because L1's prior is what justifies Round 19 Phase 1.

L1_crosscheck.not_covered: which exact GnuPG minor version emits the short 'GnuPG v1' form. C3 did not pin it to a release and does not assert one; the source check L8 3.2 performed for keygen_set_std_prefs() was not repeated for armor.c.
L1_crosscheck.recommended_action: correct F6/F7's numbers and window in round18/L1-toolchain/RESULTS.md section 6 and its ledger entry, marking the old figures superseded rather than deleting them. NOT done by C3 - outside this lane's write scope.

crypt_rsa_finding.headline: 3301's own cryptographically-signed messages name Perl, twice, two years apart - and both PASS signature verification
crypt_rsa_finding.why_it_matters: This is self-declared, signed, dated evidence for a Perl environment. It is far stronger support for Round 19's G2 (Perl 5.14 rand/srand) prior than any distro-version argument, and nobody in this repository has cited it as toolchain evidence.

messages.prose_quote: Here is a message that has been encrypted with RSA (the Crypt::RSA Perl module available in CPAN)
messages.data_dumper: the message pastes `$VAR1 = bless( { 'e' => 65537, 'n' => '...', 'Version' => '1.99', 'Identity' => '...' }, 'Crypt::RSA::Key::Public' );` - that `$VAR1 = bless(...)` form is literally Perl's Data::Dumper default output, so the author ran a Perl script and dumped the key structure straight into a signed message
messages.also_contains: 3301's OWN statement of the authenticity test: 'There are many fake messages out there. Only messages signed with public key ID 7A35090F are valid.' - which is the very test corpus G-02 exists to operationalise, stated by the keyholder, in a message that PASSes

crypt_rsa_finding.module_version_pinned: Crypt::RSA 1.99 (the module's own armor Version field, emitted by the library, on both messages)
crypt_rsa_finding.dating: both fall inside the GnuPG 1.4.11 window this lane bounded (2012-01-05 to 2014-04-02)
crypt_rsa_finding.what_this_is_not: It does not establish that the Liber Primus keystream came from Perl. It establishes that the author had a working Perl + CPAN environment in January 2012 and still in January 2014, by their own signed statement and by the library's own machine-emitted armor.
crypt_rsa_finding.lead_not_claim: Crypt::RSA::ES::OAEP draws its padding randomness through Crypt::Random. Whether that dependency chain is a plausible source for any 3301 keystream is a question for a generator lane, not a claim made here.

I_01.verdict: INDECISIVE - round18's verdict stands, unchanged by C3
I_01.summary: Where the SOFTWARE chose, the two keys agree; where a HUMAN chose, they differ. Key size 4096 vs 2048, expiry policy none vs ONE DAY, revocation never vs 2012-01-22 (reason 0x03 'no longer used'). The matching preference lists are exactly GnuPG 1.4.x/2.0.x keygen_set_std_prefs() defaults, which in January 2012 describes most new OpenPGP keys on Earth.
I_01.c3_note_1: The CicadaPG v.3301 armor header found in C3's L1 cross-check proves the author edited armor output in 2017. It does NOT weaken the INDECISIVE verdict, because that verdict rests on KEY PREFERENCE PACKETS set in January 2012 - five years earlier and a different part of the format. Recorded explicitly so the two findings are not later welded into a claim neither supports.
I_01.c3_note_2: The base-rate control is still missing and still matters. Round 18's attempt used four live project keys, none created in January 2012, and a live key's UID self-signature is REISSUED on every edit, so a keyserver copy shows the preferences of the last edit rather than of creation. A properly matched control needs keys whose self-sigs are frozen in 2012 - abandoned or revoked keys. Not sourced by round18 and not by C3.
I_01.arithmetic_correction_restated: AUDITOR-LOOP-2026-07-28.md and LEDGER.json I-01 both say the key was revoked 'seven days after the first 3301 image'. The first image is 2012-01-04, so the revocation is 18 days after it and the creation 8. Seven days is the gap between 3301's key creation (2012-01-05) and mruzuki's (2012-01-12) - the right number attached to the wrong anchor.
I_01.standing_constraint: No person is named as Cicada 3301. Public lawful sources only. Breach-DB and people-search lookups were declined in advance and not run.
